articles.title: Sony’s PlayStation Vue streaming TV service launches today in New York City, Chicago, and Philadelphia
articles.summary: $50 a month might let you really cut the cord this time
articles.body: Sony’s attempt to compete with cable TV starts today: the long-awaited PlayStation Vue TV streaming service is now available for PS3 and PS4 owners in New York, Philadelphia, and Chicago. Much like Dish’s new Sling TV service, Vue lets you pay a monthly fee to get live access to a variety of broadcast network channels as well as networks that are typically only available from cable providers. Probably the two most important factors for any service like Vue are price and channel lineup, and the network lineup Sony has on board is impressive. Sony has deals set up with CBS, Fox, NBC, Discovery, Scripps, Turner, Viacom, and AMC — that adds up to more than 85 total distinct channels. Of course, that won’t come cheap. The entry package costs $49.99 per month and covers about 50 different channels. For most Vue users, that $50 package should be sufficient, as it covers a whole host of some of the most popular channels you’ll get in any cable package. It includes local broadcast channels from NBC, Fox, and CBS as well as cable networks like TNT, TBS, USA, MTV, Animal Planet, BET, FX, Comedy Central, AMC (starting next month), and many more. It’s an impressive lineup — when I thought about how I use cable TV currently, I realized that the entry level Vue package would cover a huge chunk of the shows I like to keep up with. Unfortunately, there’s one huge hole in Sony’s lineup — ABC. That means no ESPN, no Disney, or even the local ABC affiliate so you can keep up with Modern Family. It’s a real shame, as it keeps Vue from truly being a one-stop service you can use to cut the cord for good — we’re keeping our fingers crossed that ABC and Sony will be able to come to an agreement sooner than later. Still, there’s a lot to like in Vue’s basic channel lineup. Sony’s $59.99 step-up “Core” package is mostly aimed at sports fans — it includes national sports networks BTN and the Golf Channel as well as regional sports networks like New York’s YES and Comcast SportsNet in Chicago and Philadelphia. There’s also a $69.99 “Elite” package that mostly adds a bunch of niche channels; for most users, the standard package will probably be more than enough. [Image: The last piece of the puzzle for Vue is the interface, and fortunately Sony has put together something that’s a lot nicer and easier to use than what you’ll get from most cable providers these days. When you start Vue, you’ll automatically be in live TV mode on whatever channel you were on previously, just like turning on most cable boxes. When you jump into the interface, the live TV keeps playing in the background and you’re presented with your “timeline” — what you’re currently watching, what’s up next, and (if you scroll backwards), what you’ve watched recently. From there, you can scroll down into the other main ways Vue organizes your content: My Shows, Favorite Channels, and Live TV. They’re pretty self-explanatory — the first two collect any show or channel that you save while browsing through Vue, while Live TV shows you every single program that is currently airing. By default, all these areas let you scroll left to right to view the programs and channels you look at most often, but you can also jump into a bigger, grid-style overview that gives more of a bird’s-eye view of what’s available. Adding things to your lists is quite simple — at any time while you have a network or show highlighted, you can hit R1 to save it. Since Sony’s DVR is cloud-based, you don’t have to worry about any conflicts when saving items for later — and once you’ve saved a show, you’ll have access to all episodes of the show that have aired in the last 28 days. Vue also makes the last three days of “popular programming” available without needing to schedule it for a recording, making it easier to catch up on a premiere you might have forgotten to save. [Image: Other ways to find content include a traditional search; recommendations based on viewing habits, as well as what’s popular with other Vue users; filters that let you find shows by picking genre, style, rating, length, and so on; and a twist on the traditional cable box guide. Instead of a guide that shows time going from left to right and an endless stream of channels, Vue’s guide puts channels left to right, with all of your favorites right up front. You can easily scroll back in time and “catch up” on shows that you’ve missed (assuming the network has given users the rights to do so). It’s not the most bare-bones or simple interface, and there are lots of options for finding content, but the main categories — live TV, favorite shows, and favorite channels — are probably what most users will use most of the time. Fortunately, they’re simple to understand and right up front. Since it’s so easy to favorite channels and shows, those areas will fill up with content fast. That’s Sony’s vision for the future of TV. It’s probably the most comprehensive, over-the-top TV service to launch thus far, and it’s the one that gives the most people the best option for cutting cable entirely — or it will when it launches nationwide. Sony says more cities will be online before the end of the year, but they didn’t quite give specifics on when it’ll be available to everyone in the US. Of course, notable caveats abound: right now, it’s only available on the PS4 and PS3, with an iPad version coming later. While Sony’s consoles are popular video streaming devices, there’s still a swath of other set-top boxes that can’t use Sony’s service. And the lack of ABC and its associated networks leaves a big hole in Vue’s channel lineup. That said, a channel lineup that’s still quite strong and an intelligent and customizable interface (even if it is a bit busy) are two big wins for Sony’s first efforts here. We’re hoping that Sony and Dish’s Sling push each other to get even better, and that Apple shows up with its rumored service soon. The more competition we see, the better it’ll be for those who want to cut the cord. If you want to give it a shot and live in one of the launch cities, Sony’s offering a free week trial.

articles.title: Huawei’s first trifold is a great phone that you shouldn’t buy
articles.summary: Huawei’s Mate XT is a fun first-gen trifold that’s too expensive, doesn’t support Google apps, and is limited to 4G.
articles.body: Let’s get one thing out of the way immediately: you shouldn’t buy Huawei’s trifold phone, the Mate XT. And that’s alright, because you probably couldn’t if you wanted to — while it’s no longer exclusive to China, it’s only on sale in a handful of countries, and not in the US or Europe. Besides, I can reel off a list of major problems with the Mate XT: at almost $4,000 it’s far too expensive, it doesn’t have native support for Google apps (though you can get around that more easily than you might think), it’s limited to 4G, and there are some pretty obvious reasons to worry about its durability. Any one of those individually would be a good reason to steer clear of buying the Mate XT. Taken together, they’re insurmountable. But this isn’t a phone you’re meant to buy, at least not outside China. It’s a phone you’re meant to gawk at on the internet, to marvel at Huawei’s technological prowess, to ooh and ahh about its many and varied folds. This is Huawei showing off, proving to the world that it’s still got it. And in fairness, it has. [Product: Huawei Mate XT | As I sit and write this — more than six months after Huawei first released the Mate XT in China — it’s still the only one of its kind. Rumor has it that Samsung has a trifold ready to show off this year, but it hasn’t yet. And by the time it does, odds are Huawei will have spent a full year as the only player in the game. That might ring alarm bells in your head. This must be undercooked tech, you think, rushed out the door to beat everyone else to market. But the most surprising thing about the Mate XT is that it only occasionally feels first-gen. [Image: This is the only way to display three apps at once, with one in a floating window. There’s a hint of it in the multitasking, which refuses to allow you to fully open three apps at a time, pinning each to one of the three screen segments. Or when the fully open screen often doesn’t quite go entirely flat, which is more annoying than any crease will ever be. And you notice it when you open the phone, or close it, and the app you’re using seems to briefly reboot itself, losing your spot in a long article or (once, infuriatingly) discarding a Letterboxd review that was almost entirely finished. I’ve learned not to change the configuration while doing something, just to be safe. But for the most part, these just don’t really matter. After several weeks using the Mate XT as my main phone, my primary impression is that it delivers on its promise, effectively offering three different devices in one. [Image: [Image: [Image: Fully closed, this is simply a regular phone with a 6.4-inch display. At 12.8mm thick, it has a little heft to it, but not unduly so — it’s less than a millimeter thicker than Samsung’s Z Fold 6. It’s solid, and weighty, and even the cameras are decent. It’s as good a phone in this form as Samsung’s foldable, so long as you can live with sideloading the Play Store. When I’m reading a long article or trying to keep up in the editorial Slack channels, I open the phone up to a 7.9-inch, squarish display that’s a pretty close match for what other foldables offer. For me, this is the least useful setup of the three, a reminder that current book-style foldables offer something I don’t really want most of the time, extra screen space in all the wrong places. But that’s what the Mate XT’s full screen is for. Flipping one more section nets me a full 10.2-inch display, making this a thin, lightweight tablet I can fold up and fit in my pocket. It’s wider than it is tall, a close match for the aspect ratios in most streaming apps, ideal for watching videos and playing games, tripling the screen real estate for wide-screen entertainment. I haven’t traveled much in the time I’ve been working on this review, but this is a phone crying out for rail commutes and long-haul flights, a big-screen Balatro machine that fits in your pocket, not your backpack. [Image: [Image: Nine times out of ten, I use the Mate XT like a regular ol’ phone, and that extra screen space is probably wasted on me. But I don’t travel all that much, or make a habit of gaming on my phone; I wouldn’t make the most of this outside a handful of plane rides a year. Maybe you wouldn’t either, but I imagine anyone who already gets regular use out of both a phone and a tablet is feeling a little pull of temptation to merge them into one. The main thing people have asked me about the Mate XT, once they get over the foldiness of it all, is whether the battery sucks. In my experience, it absolutely doesn’t. The 5,600mAh capacity proves more than capable of lasting a full day (and then some), but I’ll refer you back to the previous paragraph — I’m not spending all day with the phone fully open. 5,600mAh is a decent battery for a phone, but a small one for a tablet, so if that’s your main use case, then you should expect to feel a bit more of a pinch. [Image: This exposed screen edge certainly feels like a failure point. The second thing people ask is how likely it is to break. And compared to a regular phone, the answer is pretty likely! There’s a whole extra failure point in the second hinge, and no IP rating, so you can’t trust it to survive either water or dust. I’m more worried that one part of the soft, flexible screen is always exposed to the outside world. It’s going to get nicks, scratches, and dents, and there’s nothing you can do about it. My review unit already has a couple, and I’ve been babying the thing. I’d say you shouldn’t buy this unless you can afford to replace it, but again: you probably shouldn’t buy it at all. Maybe you should buy the next one. Or the one after that. Or one a few generations down the line. Or just the first one that isn’t made by Huawei, because fantastic as the company’s hardware can be, I’m still not convinced it’s worth giving up proper Google support. But while the Mate XT may be the first trifold, I’m confident it won’t be the last. And this hardware, with Google and 5G, for two-thirds the price, and a generation or two of durability improvements? You should buy that phone. [Image: Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: The Best LEGO Disney Sets in 2026
articles.summary: There are no shortage of Disney-themed LEGO sets, but these are our picks for the best ones to pick up right now.
articles.body:
The Disney/LEGO partnership goes back a long way, and it encompasses a wide variety of sets. Some of these are meant to appeal mostly for kids. Others are bigger and more complex builds meant for display rather than play, and can easily be appreciated by adults. In any case, here are the best LEGO Disney sets that you can buy as of August 2026. To make this guide specific and helpful, we are classifying "LEGO Disney" as the sets inspired by the Walt Disney Animation Studios and Disney Parks.

LEGO LEGO The Nightmare Before Christmas

For the blurb-averse, these are our favorite Disney LEGO sets. If you want more info on any of them, keep on reading.

The greatest robot couple of all time come packaged together for a single price. These models are small, but not so small that they skimp on LEGO's signature attention to detail. Wall-E comes with a garbage cube that fits in its torso, as well as a boot with a plant growing out of it. The set also comes with tiny recreations of M-O and Hal the cockroach, who can perch on WALL-E's shoulder.

This model of The Black Pearl demonstrates LEGO design expertise when it comes to boats, ships, and other maritime vehicles. The set depicts the Pearl's "cursed" appearance, with its signature black, ripped sails. The ship comes with eight minifigures, and its interiors include a treasure room and a fully outfitted Captain's quarters, where you can play out the first confrontation between Elizabeth and Barbossa.

Cruella's luxury car is iconic, made famous by the chase scene at the climax of 101 Dalmatians. It's a monstrous thing colored in decadent red, with oversized wheels that dwarf Cruella herself. This set also comes with a Cruella minifigure (some of the best, most detailed work I've ever seen on an individual minifigure) plus a tiny Dalmatian puppy (Penny).

The cutest entry on this list allows you to build Patch, Penny, Rolly, Pepper, Lucky or Freckles —or, if you're feeling particularly ambitious, you can create a customized dalmatian of your own. This model is fully poseable, allowing your puppy to stand, sit, or lie down in a variety of positions.

Pixar's longtime mascot has his own LEGO set thanks to the LEGO Ideas initiative . The lamp is spring-loaded, allowing it to 'bounce' if you move it up and down, and it comes with the trademark Pixar ball, filled with little Easter eggs from their movies. There's also a major Easter egg in the lamp itself, but you'll have to build it to know what it is.

We built this set for its launch , and we loved looking at all the little, thoughtful details packed into every inch. In addition to the expected minifigures, there's the entire roster of magical household objects. There's a ballroom, a dining room, a study, and the infamous West Wing. The castle is perfect for re-enacting and posing classic scenes.

We reviewed this set for its launch , and it has the perfect amounts of whimsical and weird. It's three builds in one – Halloween Town Hall, Jack Skellington's House, and Spiral Hill – rendered in Burton's trademark, off-kilter style, with impossible-looking, angled walls. They're perfect display pieces for a delightful Halloween or a morbid Christmas.

Brightly colored and extremely cute, this LEGO Stitch wears a Hawaiian shirt and comes with two accessories: a flower tucked behind its ear and an ice cream cone in its paw. Its ears are articulable, and even though the age range is 9+, an adult would have a great time building and displaying a set like this one.

There's also a newer Stitch model available here ; it's the same size and scope as the prior model, and it depicts Stitch with a ti-leaf skirt, a ukelele, and a smaller model of Scrump.

Nearly a foot tall, this recreation of a young Simba has a big smile and a rounded, cute appearance, with its haunches coiled like he's ready to pounce. It reminds me a bit of those composite mosaic photos, where when you look closer at one, you realize that it's hundreds of little pictures that combine to form a large image. Similarly, this build is such a good fascimile that it looks seamless from a distance. It's only when you get closer that you see its LEGO.

Adorable and precious, this Brickheadz of Eeyore has movable ears and hindquarters, and it's separable from the baseplate it's mounted on. It's only $13, which is a rarity and a steal for a LEGO set – especially a set with third-party branding.

Main Street, U.S.A. is the first thing you see upon entering Disneyland. A burst of mid-century American nostalgia, it was Walt's attempt to replicate his Missouri hometown.

This set includes four iconic landmarks: the Fire Station, the Disney Family apartment, the Crystal Arcade, and the Emporium. You also get an old-timey fire truck and a popcorn cart. Minifigures include Mickey Mouse, Minnie Mouse, and the long-standing acapella quartet The Dapper Dans.

According to LEGO's official store , 72 LEGO Disney sets are available for purchase as of August 2026, across multiple age groups and skill levels. Give the entire catalog a look if none of these sets do it for you.

LEGO and Disney are a terrific match, in the sense that both companies cast a wide, welcoming net. Disney is not in the business of making children' s e ntertainment ; Disney is in the business of making family entertainment . That distinction is crucial, because the implicit intent is for everyone, regardless of age or maturity, to enjoy Disney at the level they are cognitively able.

A small child might like the bright colors and funny characters. An older kid might like the subversion of expectations. And an adult might enjoy Disney as a piece of nostalgic Americana, through which they can revisit their childhoods. Disney is cross-generational, because it appeals to everyone through common, shared experiences.

And LEGO, meanwhile, has nostalgia built into its very ethos. The "System" – the idea that every new brick fits with the old bricks from 50-60 years ago, ensures that bricks and sets and models can pass down, constituting a hobby that moves from parent to child. And now that LEGO, like Disney, is directly appealing to adults as much as kids, the company is more successful than ever.

In related news, check out our picks for the best LEGO Marvel sets (Disney acquired Marvel in 2009), as well as the best LEGO Star Wars sets (Disney acquired Star Wars in 2012).

Kevin Wong is a contributing freelancer for IGN, specializing in LEGO. He's also been published in Complex, Engadget, Gamespot, Kotaku, and more. Follow him on Twitter at @kevinjameswong .

articles.body:
Looking to enhance your smile this year? Great news: Amazon has reduced a bunch of electric toothbrushes for UK customers, including Philips’ award-winning Sonicare range.

With prices starting as low as £45 and discounts reaching 60%, it’s a great time to invest in your pearly whites, and you’ll reap the rewards for years to come.

articles.title: Onimusha: Way of the Sword Video Review - IGN
articles.summary: Onimusha: Way of the Sword reviewed by Will Borger on PS5, also available on Xbox Series X, PlayStation 5, and Switch 2."It’s a testament to Onimusha: Way of the Sword’s combat that I could beat it without using some of the systems designed to help you progress – not because you don’t need them, but because it leaves room for you to truly understand its action and overcome their absence through sheer determination. Even if I hadn’t intentionally made things harder for myself, though, I still would have loved spending time with the charismatic denizens of this world, all of whom are as well acted as they are animated. I still would have thought that Musashi himself was one of the coolest, most interesting protagonists in any video game, and I would have loved going on this journey with him. I still would have savored the creative fights against dozens of impressive bosses. My journey reflected Musashi's, and Onimusha made that possible. The best part of life is the challenge. You have to learn to love the fight."

articles.title: One of This Year’s Best Open-world RPGs Is a Bloody Cocktail of Interesting Ideas and Well-written Characters - The Blood of Dawnwalker Review
articles.summary: This impressive, bloody cocktail is one of the year’s best open-world RPGs.
articles.body:
Ever since I first got infected with Porphyric Hemophilia in The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind or ran amok in Los Angeles in Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines, I’ve been patiently waiting for an open-world vampire RPG that I could really sink my teeth into. Frustratingly, despite numerous attempts in all those years, I hadn’t found anything that quenched that long-standing thirst. With The Blood of Dawnwalker, an RPG that shares a ton of DNA with The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt made by some of its former developers, my hunt is finally over. Not only does it take the vampire fantasy to the neck-xt level, it also smartly finds workarounds for some of the limitations that can be a bit annoying (like having to stay out of the light), and introduces other interesting and clever ideas along the way. The day/night cycle that has you switching between human and vampire consistently makes for compelling questing, the limited time you’re given to complete your adventure makes even minor decisions carry enormous stakes , and the numerous ways to make its bloody tale your own have motivated me to rise from the coffin and replay this journey more than any game has in quite a long time. This is the vampire RPG I’ve been waiting for and I find myself entirely under its spell.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a third-person action RPG that puts you in the shoes of a no-longer-fully-human protagonist with long hair and facial scars who runs around using swords and magic to kill monsters in a gritty, dark fantasy setting. Perhaps not the most original premise from a bunch of former Witcher devs, but hey, if it ain’t broke, don’t pull it off the stuffed unicorn. You play as Coen of Laslea, whose town is taken over by vampires, then through a series of unfortunate events, is infected with vampirism and begins practicing the dark art of witchcraft on the same day. Tough break! Naturally, you set out on a roughly 40-hour quest for revenge against those evil bloodsuckers, using your unique abilities as a Dawnwalker (someone who has all the strengths and weaknesses of a vampire by night but a human by day) to save the valley of Vale Sangora from the clutches of evil.

The Blood of Dawnwalker - Skill Tree Menu Screenshots

While the premise is pretty basic, Dawnwalker excels in the telling, with a cast of extremely well-written characters across the board, a world that’s filled with more mysteries than you could ever hope to uncover during your time-constrained journey, and some weirdly impressive arguments for why maybe vampires should be in charge of the world that made me pause to wonder if I was, in fact, the baddie. I instantly found myself eagerly spending time with Anca, the kind witch with a tragic past who split her time between either teaching me latin and magic or shamelessly flirting with me. Meanwhile, Crake, the rebel leader with a tendency to be heinously cruel in service of the cause, and Lacra, an allied vampire who casually committed war crimes half the time I hung out with her, managed to win me over despite being huge pains in my ass. Even the primary villains, like Brencis, who envisions a world ruled by vampires, and Ambrus, the footsoldier who revels in the displacement of the hierarchy of nobility and fancies a gentleman’s duel, were all incredibly compelling figures.

Dawnwalker’s best and most unique feature, quite appropriately for a game all about vampires, is its day/night cycle and the time mechanics built around it. As a spell-slinging human by day who turns into a blood-sucking monster by night, just about everything you do changes depending on the time of day. For example, in your human form you’ll guzzle down food and medicine to heal yourself, battle with swords and a fistful of witchcraft spells, and move around the old fashioned way by running, jumping, climbing, and whatnot. As a vampire, all that food and medicine is completely useless to you and your health can only be restored by consuming blood, plus you’ll primarily fight with your bare claws and gain a whole bunch of neat movement options – that includes teleporting around as a cloud of smoke, walking on walls and ceilings like the creepy little creature you are, and even turning into a wolf.

That means instead of building one loadout of armor, weapons, consumables, and abilities you’re happy with, Dawnwalker requires you to maintain two separate builds, which gave my stat-obsessed brain twice as much to joyfully tinker with. My vampire build was an absolute terror on the battlefield, with all my abilities centered around feeding off enemies to continually restore my health, and I sought out as many items as possible that increased my claw damage to turn myself into an unkillable unarmed freak of nature. Meanwhile, my human build primarily relied on high risk/high reward spells that put a whole bunch of nasty status effects on my foes at the cost of draining my own life and making me quite squishy. These two extremely different ways to play meant I was almost sitting forward during combat. Best of all, each of these loadouts is kept separate and automatically toggled between when you switch forms, so you don’t have to manually swap out all your armor and weapons twice a day.

Speaking of fighting, you’ll be doing quite a bit of that, since you’ll primarily solve your problems in Vale Sangora with the pointy end of your blade. The combat is quite good, with the caveat that it has a bit of a steep learning curve I suspect will be equally divisive. The main way in which it sets itself apart from most RPGs of this kind is that it uses a directional parry system where you have to match the direction the enemy is swinging, which kinda reminded me of For Honor. You can also just block attacks like normal, but doing so is fairly impractical (at least on higher difficulties) since it drains your stamina and doesn’t provide the openings for counterattacks that are so vital to success.

It sounds simple, but it took me longer than I’d like to admit to feel comfortable with it. The first handful of hours were fairly frustrating, and I frequently found myself fumbling through most combat encounters while cursing my ancestors. But there was light at the end of that tunnel – once I got over the hump and this system clicked, I grew to not only like it, but also feel pretty damn good at it. Now I’m able to down even the most formidable hordes without breaking a sweat, and that mastery felt earned beyond my stats going up. (Granted, I insist on playing most games on the hardest difficulty, so it’s quite possible I was just making things especially hard on myself and you’ll have an easier time from the jump.)

Aside from parrying, though, you’ll be using a pretty familiar bag of tricks for an action game like this, with a combination of standard attacks, special maneuvers that are specific to whichever weapon you’ve got equipped, and a bunch of abilities you can activate on a cooldown. Naturally, all of this will differ depending on whether or not you’re in human or vampire form, which goes a long way toward keeping things from getting too repetitive. For example, as a human, I fancied status effect spells that drained health and stunned enemies at the cost of my own life force, but as a vampire, I’d pummel things mercilessly with my bare hands and banshee shriek in my enemy’s face if I was feeling cheeky.

That said, these bouts definitely have some relatively minor but pretty obvious places they could improve. For example, the lock-on function consistently gave me trouble when trying to target a specific enemy, and it stayed annoying no matter how long I practiced with it. The camera could also get caught in odd spots in a way that was similarly aggravating. And while the variety of enemies you encounter is pretty good overall, the more common beasts you run into in the wild, like wolves and boars, appear way too frequently – by the end of my time with Coen, I was fully pissed off at the mere sight of the overpopulated canines.

While adventuring out in the world, certain activities are only available at specific times of day. For example, you’ll need access to your vampire form’s superior movement capabilities in order to climb to the top of lookout towers and add nearby points of interest to your map, while rituals that require blood magic are only available in human form. But even activities available at any time, like most side quests, can have drastically different outcomes depending on which form you take. Some characters will be less likely to trust you if you interact with them in vampire form, while some areas might be inaccessible if you choose to tackle it while human. If you really muck things up, your character might just straight up murder a super important NPC because you stupidly interacted with them while in a state of overwhelming blood thirst. Not that I ever did that at all, because I’m super smart and very good at video games.

The most interesting aspect of The Blood of Dawnwalker’s day/night cycle is how it ties the passage of time to specific actions you take, giving you a finite amount of time to complete your overarching quest. After the story’s opening chapter, you’ll have exactly 30 days to bring Brencis’ rule to an end, and that deadline is stressfully enforced as almost every action you take costs a certain amount of time to complete. There isn’t a ticking timer or anything – in fact, you can freely explore the world or just stand around idly as long as you want without time passing. Instead, time is treated as a resource: want to buy the next level in a particular skill? Well, in addition to the skill points required, you’ll also have to pay the much more costly price of the hours it takes you to train in it. Want to help that old man with his minor problem because you’re roleplaying as a good person? Fine! Go right ahead… but that’s one fewer segment of time you’ve got to potentially complete a more substantial sidequest.

At first I thought I might find this limitation irritating, since I quite enjoy taking my time to smell the roses and mark every checkbox off my list in these kinds of open-worlds, but I quickly realized how treating time as a currency makes just about every aspect of Dawnwalker better. No matter how hard you try, you won’t have enough hours to complete every side quest, buy every skill, or tie up every loose end as well as you’d like, which means you’re forced to compromise, pick your battles, and make hard but impactful decisions almost constantly. For example, early on in my travels, I talked my way into a prison camp to get some intel from a prisoner there, one I would have gone out of my way to rescue under normal circumstances. But when I saw that it would cost me three pips of time to do so (each day has 16 total), I decided to leave him to rot instead. I was forced to make compromises like this every step of the way, all in service of ensuring I had enough time for the important stuff, and I regularly found myself surprised at my own decisions. Fittingly, it made me feel like I truly was letting the darkness of my new vampiric abilities compromise my humanity in my quest for revenge. It’s brutal, nerve-wracking, and completely awesome.

This harrowing time-crunch ultimately has a pretty enormous impact on how your journey ends as well. I won’t spoil anything, but alternate endings will only open up to you if you’ve met certain characters or taken specific actions. On my first playthrough, there were entire supporting characters and story components I completely missed out on, and I didn’t realize the scope of what I hadn’t seen until I took an entirely different approach on my second playthrough. In a third (much shorter) playthrough, I just went for a brute force approach to see what would happen if I rushed straight to the end without meeting anyone while leveling up as little as possible, and I was not disappointed by the hilarious result. This is one of those games where I not only wanted to play through multiple times, but it almost felt mandatory in order to see everything Vale Sangora had in store. I can’t remember the last time I’ve felt that way about an RPG.

One thing I often worry about with open-world RPGs is just how bad their performance and technical bugs might be, and The Blood of Dawnwalker thankfully finds itself on the less egregious side of the spectrum. Sure, on a standard PlayStation 5 it’s got the occasional framerate wonkiness, the camera sometimes clips through stuff in awkward ways, and an enemy will occasionally go right through the floor when you kill it – but almost everything I saw like that was pretty minor and uncommon, and I never had a single hard crash, broken questline, or anything else frustrating like that. The worst thing I encountered with regularity were blurry textures on characters’ clothes (or sometimes detail in their faces), which would distractingly never smooth out from time to time. Importantly, the version I played did not include the 60fps performance mode that was recently announced , so I can’t say just how well it holds up on that front, but I wasn’t particularly bothered by the 30FPS quality mode since it usually looked and ran well enough anyway.

articles.title: Housemarque Co-Founder Ilari Kuittinen Announces Exit from Saros Developer After 31 Years
articles.summary: Housemarque co-founder Ilari Kuittinen has announced his exit from the PlayStation studio after 31 years.
articles.body:
Housemarque co-founder Ilari Kuittinen has announced his exit from the PlayStation studio after 31 years.

The Saros developer shared the news with its followers with Kuittinen's final message, confirming today as his last with the team. It's a lengthy letter to fans that saw the studio head wave goodbye after overseeing the launch of arcade-y classics like Saros , Returnal , Resogun , and more.

"After 33 years in the games industry and 31 incredible years at Housemarque—the studio I co-founded with Harri Tikkanen—today marks my last day at the company," he said. "Starting out in 1993 with Terramarque, and then joining forces with Harri to establish Housemarque in 1995, we had a passion for games but no real blueprint for building a business. Looking back, I feel immensely fortunate. We had the luck of being in the right place at the right time during three decades of incredible industry growth, allowing us to stay fiercely independent for 26 years before finding a home within the PlayStation Studios family."

"My core purpose as a leader has always been simple: to facilitate an environment where extraordinary creators have the freedom and protection to do what they do best."

Housemarque has evolved in unique ways through the years. Though its commitment to gameplay has remained through the decades, it branched beyond simple shoot-em-ups throughout the lifecycles of the PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5 consoles.

PlayStation fans will remember when Resogun helped the PS4 launch in 2013. Twin-stick shooters like Alienation and Nex Machina would then arrive in 2016 and 2017, respectively, but Housemarque then went on to truly push the boundaries of its capabilities with its more story-driven roguelike, Returnal, for PS5 in April 2021.

Sony officially cemented the company as a PlayStation Studio later that same year, and in April of this year, it released its follow-up, Saros. Kuittinen was there for it all.

In his letter, he pointed to Housemarque's evolution into a AAA developer, its games, and its status as a pioneering Finnish game studio as three particularly noteworthy achievements he and the team have managed to accomplish. He also clarified that this isn't a sudden change; studio veteran Sami 'Haxu' Hakala took over as managing director July 1, 2026. It's something Kuittinen said he, Hakala, and the rest of the team have been carefully planning behind-the-scenes.

"Housemarque’s strategy and creative vision are in exceptional hands," he added. "As for me? After 33 continuous years without a major break, I am taking a rare and well-deserved breather trying to find out how good I am at doing nothing! To Harri, our partners at SIE, our global industry friends, and every single team member who has ever walked through Housemarque’s doors: thank you for making the past 31 years the privilege of a lifetime."

A final message from our co-founder, Ilari Kuittinen pic.twitter.com/ubf0yZJBWq — Housemarque (@Housemarque) August 31, 2026

A final message from our co-founder, Ilari Kuittinen pic.twitter.com/ubf0yZJBWq

IGN gave Saros a 7/10 review upon its launch earlier this year. We said, at the time, that it "tries at an interesting and ambitious story it isn't always able to effectively tell, but Housemarque has once again proved that its bullet-hell sensibilities mesh incredibly well with fluid and challenging action."

Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

articles.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker Review, Gameplay Impressions, Videos and Top Features
articles.summary: The Blood of Dawnwalker from developer Rebel Wolves is one of those games with the blueprint to be a breakout hit.
articles.body:
The Blood of Dawnwalker from developer Rebel Wolves is one of those games with the blueprint to be a breakout hit.

A third-person action RPG, the vampiric romp certainly passes the early eye test and has some eyebrow-raising pedigree. With involvement from some behind an all-time classic like The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, it's flying more under the proverbial radar than it probably should.

Tack on an extremely interesting mechanic governing the game's story and giving players tense choices to make, and Dawnwalker might just carve out its own bloody niche while demanding attention during a crowded release calendar.

A dark fantasy, medieval Southeast Europe is as moody, shadowy and immersive as one might expect, both in visuals and sound design.

Not that there aren't impressive lighting displays within forests and villages dense with realistic swaying fauna during the daytime. But players know what they're getting themselves into: This is a grisly game bathed in reds and grays and some, at times, uncomfortable detail in terms of wounds and realistic exchanges between combatants…or assailants and victims.

On first pass, combat looks Witcher-esque, no doubt. There's the usual weapon-based array of things going on and the accompanying meters and ability usage to match.

The game's day-night cycle dramatically changes the gameplay. When the sun is up, the swords come out to play. A four-direction melee system is one way players can go about things, which loops in things like blocks and parries. Think, Kingdom Come: Deliverance.

But players can also choose a "traditional" combat mode, which consumes more stamina. Things are faster here and directions don't matter, so it's more arcade-like or what one might expect from a standard third-person game.

Switching between the two styles is mostly preference, it seems. But both do their job well and are fun enough. That doesn't sound glowing, but things can get repetitive, especially if enemy variety doesn't jump often. But at the same time, basic weapon combat was a weakness for Witcher 3, too…and we all know how that turned out.

When the sun is down and night reigns, players have vampire combat abilities, like biting and regeneration, plus vampire-like traversal, like walking on walls.

Naturally, nighttime tends to be more about stealth while en route to a target. Or can be. It's fun to get excited when the sun starts to set, knowing things are about to get a shakeup.

And yes, this is a vampire game. If the player doesn't satisfy bloodlust at night, meaning feed on animals (or humans for better healing…but corruption that eventually has negative effects), the protagonist will take over the game and go do it himself to the nearest human or enemy. These victims could be as important as quest-givers or merchants, forever altering the game, too.

The stakes (vampire pun, sorry) are high, then, to say the least.

There's an underlying tension to the game, too, from a pacing standpoint. Every decision matters, in terms of how to complete goals and in what order

Every day and night gets cut into eight time segments. Exploring the open world doesn't count, but every quest has a time cost attached to it.

Call it a nice capper on a fitting gameplay loop that is, ultimately, fun to experiment with and enjoyable.

Players assume the role of Coen, a Dawnwalker and they enter a tale that includes blood tithes, nasty dictators and a hunt for survival.

Without going into spoiler territory, it's a great time. On its own, the story might be about what onlookers expect. But the narrative devices around it, including choosing which quests to tackle and which to skip, how and when, really adds an exclamation point. There's always something to do, find or interesting characters to meet, too.

Quest variety is peak here. There's no distinction between main and side quests. Players can choose to be a detective, dive into more narrative-based stuff through dialogue trees or even run off into the open world to help strangers, slay mini-bosses or figure out traversal puzzles, to name a few items out there.

And yes, it certainly seems like there are quests that add up to more time than players actually have to complete the game. So, player choice is critical, and indeed, one run through the game could feel quite a bit different from the next.

Some might yearn for the overarching, expansive and kingdom-and-region-spanning romp of a game like Witcher 3. But the scope here is still impressive, the open world grand and more agency to how a tale unfolds is immersive in its own role-playing right.

That open world is huge, with organic-feeling events, helpful viewpoints to unlock more things on the map and plenty of little side activities.

The day-night cycle impacts the deep progression systems, too. There are human, vampire and shared perk trees to course through and make choices.

Dawnwalker runs well with the expected stuff going on in its options menus, both in terms of accessibility and must-haves like different camera perspective options.

Dawnwalker is one of the unexpected breakout hits of the year.

Again, it's a little surprising that there wasn't more hype here. Yes, the combat can be a little repetitive at times, but it's very much a Witcher 3 situation: The rest is just that good.

A better-than-expected open world in an age of open world fatigue, with tension-riddled decisions underlying something as simple as deciding to do a quest (or not) and an immersive overall package make Dawnwalker a treat.

Given the stacked release calendar for this end-of-year stretch, Dawnwalker might not be an immediate hit, but it's got a Witcher 3-like staying power that will only get better with time.

articles.title: Mondo Unveils The Real Ghostbusters: Louis Tully & Grundel Figures
articles.summary: Mondo continues to cater to The Real Ghostbusters fans with high-end figures worthy of the classic cartoon, and we've got an exclusive first look at their latest release.
articles.body:
While there's no shortage of Ghostbusters collectibles on the market, the pickings are a little slimmer when it comes to toys based specifically on the classic The Real Ghostbusters cartoon. Fortunately, Mondo has been busy filling that void in recent years, and they're back with another exclusive set of 1:12 figures featuring an iconic Ghostbuster paired with a terrifying ghost. Or several ghosts, in this case.

Mondo's latest The Real Ghostbusters set pairs everyone's favorite annoying accountant, Louis Tully, with the ghost known as Grundel. This set even includes a Grundel Alec and a proton pack-wearing Slimer figure for good measure. IGN can exclusively debut the first photos of this timed edition set, which you can see in the slideshow gallery below:

Mondo's The Real Ghostbusters: Louis Tully & Grundel Figures - Image Gallery

In the tradition of previous Real Ghostbusters releases, the Louis Tulkly & Grundel set includes a wealth of accessories for both characters. We already mentioned the companion Slimer and Grundel Alec figures, but Louis comes with a proton pack, Ghost Trap, PKE Tracker, Ecto Goggles, and an alternate head, while Grundel includes his own interchangeable heads and hands.

The Louis Tully & Grundel set is priced at $202 and is a timed edition exclusive to Mondo's website . If previous Real Ghostbusters releases are any indication, Mondo will later offer the Louis figure on its own as a non-timed edition, but this set will be the only way to acquire Grundel. A Grundel bundle, if you will.

Previously, IGN got an exclusive first look at the Real Ghostbusters: Winston Zeddemore and Sandman set . At this point, Mondo has tackled all four main Ghostbusters and Janine, along with an SDCC-exclusive "Citizen Ghost" bundle . Every Real Ghostbusters figure is currently sold out on Mondo's website , which seems to prove there's a lot of pent-up demand for these figures.

In other collectibles news, Jim Lee's iconic X-Men art is on full display in a gorgeous new art book.

articles.title: Onslaught’s Trio of Villains The Crybaby, The Cockroach and The Butcher Look Like They Walked Right Out of Call of Duty’s Zombies Mode
articles.summary: Onslaught rips. Adam Wingard's ode to '80s action movies features stellar performances, cool villains, and a down-and-dirty feel that make it a very easy recommendation.
articles.body:
Onslaught will be released in theaters on September 4.

Onslaught is an apt title for Adam Wingard’s continuation of the world the director and co-writer Simon Barrett established early in their careers through You’re Next and The Guest , because it just never lets up. The platonic ideal of a “midnight movie,” Onslaught serves up heaping helpings of gruesome action, witty dialogue, Nazi experimentation, pro-veteran and anti-government sentiment, and three militarized Michael Myers figures hunting a community of unsuspecting trailer park residents. If all that sounds distasteful and exhausting to you, the rest of this review is not for you: you’re a lost cause and I invite you to go back to watching paint dry or whatever it is you do with your free time. For those with a taste for debaucherous mayhem in your cinema, pure and crazy… Onslaught, baby!

Over 92 rocket-powered minutes, Onslaught follows the classic “survive the night” story structure with a simple premise which Wingard imbues with all manner of schlocky adornment. At base level, Onslaught is about a trio of super-soldier experimentation subjects programmed to kill anyone in their path escaping containment and fulfilling their purpose in the desert community of Moriarty, New Mexico - the very same town at the heart of 2014’s The Guest. Onslaught finds a no-bullshit hero in Celeste (Adria Arjona), a veteran sniper struggling with PTSD and motherhood as she seeks peace at the Windy Oasis Trailer Park, where most of the movie’s back-half takes place. Celeste is quick to anger, but at least adept at directing those feelings in a constructive direction once the super-soldiers lay siege to her home. Across quiet character moments and very loud, raging action beats, Arjona carries the movie beautifully and it’s consistently fun watching her settle so easily into the action hero persona. Sarah Connor would be very proud.

With their painted faces, tactical gear and glowing eyes, the imposing trio driving Onslaught’s anarchy look like bosses that walked right out of Call of Duty’s Zombies mode. Even though they have cool codenames - The Crybaby, The Cockroach, The Butcher - there’s no discernable or relevant differences between the three once things go off the deep end. Since the action taking place at the trailer park is so narrowly focused, this is of little detriment to Onslaught, giving the characters multiple tough-to-beat foes to have to work their way through and allowing Wingard to stage cat-and-mouse games that start off especially chaotic when the trio is at full strength, and become more dread-inducing as the odds start to shift away from the trio of elite soldiers. Wingard does overplay his hand late in the game by attempting to use one of the super-soldiers as a thematic exclamation point long after Onslaught needs any more depths to plumb.

It’s the fringes of Onslaught’s idiosyncratic world that really make you lean forward. Wingard’s The Guest and Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire collaborator Dan Stevens returns here as Dr. Kammler, a third-generation Nazi scientist with a penchant for white cloaks and being dominated by his wife, Frau Kammler (Rebecca Hall). Kammler can hardly contain his sensual glee at being on the precipice of delivering the Übermensch through his experimentations at a secret government base not far from the trailer park. Stevens is always at his most interesting playing weirdos, and here, he swings for the campy fences and knocks one out of the park.

Onslaught could have used more of Stevens’ off-beat performance to really shore up the “clean-up” efforts of the shadowy organization that produced the super-soldiers, but some of that sting is lessened by the other performers who shoulder that responsibility more as the story goes. Cyrus (Drew Starkey) is deployed to monitor the soldiers’ attack on the trailer park, and from the moment we meet him zonked out of his mind in a sex mansion, he manages to walk a fun tonal line of being both in over his head and completely in control at the same time. His most interesting material comes in his interactions with Frau Kammler, who winds up being one of Onslaught’s more interesting and enigmatic figures. The power dynamic between the elderly, milky-eyed Doctor Kammler and the much-younger Frau Kammler is intriguing to try and suss out, and only becomes more perplexing as Frau Kammler and Cyrus work with each other to maintain some level of operational control over the situation at the trailer park. Where Stevens aims for broad camp in his performance, Hall is much more restrained and lends Onslaught a lot of gravity.

Wingard’s most interesting thematic work comes through how this pack of freaks, whose aggression and sadomasochistic relationships with the intent to control are easily transposable onto any number of current events, something Onslaught crystallizes in its opening montage, which tracks the American government’s relationship to global war over the last 40 years.

Celeste isn’t alone in her fight against the test subjects, and the supporting cast at the trailer park counter the bizarre team of villains with down-home charm and no shortage of one-liners. Celeste’s main ally is Josiah (Reginald VelJohnson), himself a Vietnam War vet who, despite his ferocity and bravery once things go down, is quite gentle with Celeste as a mentor figure. That, of course, doesn’t stop VelJohnson from putting his Die Hard legacy to excellent use as a quip machine and sharpshooter in the fight against the soldiers.

Wingard also throws Eric Wareheim, he of Tim and Eric fame, into the mix as Kovacks, a sloppy Moriarty cop who knows nothing of either ferocity or bravery. Onslaught has no shortage of dark comedic energy, but Wareheim’s rhythm and ineptitude are always welcome and work well to cut especially tense moments. Celeste’s sharp edges are also well-rounded off by Daisy, her young daughter whose wealthy dad picks the worst weekend possible to dump her with mom. Daisy clearly spends most of her time in more civilized company, calling Celeste “ma’am” and doing chores around the house without being asked. Blake Kennedy, the young actor who plays Daisy, is a breath of fresh air and strikes the rare balance of naturalism and precociousness that never crosses the line into interminable “kid acting.” Daisy feels like a real, good egg and any time she’s in danger, it’s impossible not to care a little more about what’s going on, especially during one sequence where she has a real close call after being separated from Celeste.

Onslaught looks and sounds great, too. Oren Soffer’s cinematography does a fantastic job of highlighting the austere natural beauty of the Moriarty, New Mexico, setting, with blazing flames, kicked-up dust, and the warm glow of the trailer park’s lights giving the action a gritty, dirty feel that works to make that setting feel more real and not just gritty for gritty’s sake. Wingard lets the supernatural strength and resilience of the super-soldiers speak for itself, resisting the urge to get overly stylistic with how he stages the action and instead covering skirmishes with a more classical, straightforward approach that reinforces its ’80s action lineage, and these efforts are supported by a clear preference towards practical special effects throughout. Matt Pusti’s synthy score gives Onslaught a pulsing energy that really underlines the clear John Carpenter influence that Wingard is celebrating here, with simple repeating melodies that especially evoke two of Carpenter and Alan Howarth’s greatest scores: Escape from New York and Prince of Darkness.

articles.title: LEGO Officially Reveals Wallace & Gromit-Themed Set
articles.summary: LEGO has officially revealed its first Wallace and Gromit-themed set, which depicts the iconic British duo in their vintage motorbike and sidecar.
articles.body:
LEGO has officially revealed its first Wallace and Gromit-themed set.

The set depicts the iconic British duo in their vintage motorbike and sidecar with references to the stop-motion movies and original clay designs. The set is up for preorder on the online LEGO Store , priced at $99.99 with a release date of October 1.

The Wallace & Gromit set is the newest addition to the LEGO Ideas line , a program where fans can submit their own original set designs. After a series of fan-voting, LEGO ultimately picks some submissions to turn into official sets.

The Wallace & Gromit set was originally designed by Sébastien Esnault and submitted to the 90s Throwback - The Next Chapter challenge , where it took home the Grand Winner prize. The official LEGO version of the set looks pretty darn similar to the original build, having simply refined the faces of the iconic duo as well as the structure of the motorbike.

To accompany the set’s reveal, LEGO released an interview with the original Fan designer on their blog. Esnault felt thematically inspired by the duo’s humor and inventiveness, and explains his specific approach to building them in brick form: “To recreate the distinctive clay look, I deliberately chose the most rounded LEGO elements wherever possible.”

The official set includes 1038 pieces, mathing out to slightly over 10 cents ber brick. It’s also marked as an 18+ set intended for adults , so expect some level of complexity.

Wallace and Gromit first used this version of the motorbike and sidecar in A Close Shave, where it’s eventually revealed to have emergency flying features. The plane features don’t seem to have made the LEGO cut, but the shape, color, and license plate are all loyal to the original design.

Images on the LEGO website show off some smaller details, including goggles that Gromit can actually wear and a dedicated motorcycle that can open and close. Easter eggs inside that hatch include box of orange crackers in the style seen throughout the series as well as a diamond referencing the iconic heist from The Wrong Trousers.

The LEGO listing has videos demonstrating some poseability in the duo’s heads and arms. Designer Esnault highlights the effort put into each character’s expressions, saying “It only takes a tiny change in their angle to transform Gromit’s expression from curious to amused or worried.” It doesn't seem like you can fully separate Gromit or Wallace from their vehicle, however, so don’t expect this set to fill the void of action figures.

Blythe (she/her) is an Audience Development Coordinator at IGN who spends way too much time in character customization screens and tracking down collectibles.

articles.title: Ubisoft May Have Accidentally Revealed the Next Nintendo Direct Date Thanks to a Just Dance Leak
articles.summary: Nintendo fans believe Ubisoft may have just revealed the date of the next Nintendo Direct, and if true, it's very soon.
articles.body:
Nintendo fans believe Ubisoft may have just revealed the date of the next Nintendo Direct, and if true, it's very soon.

Recently, a bunch of content from the new Just Dance game, Just Dance: Decades of Hits, surfaced online, prompting a response from Ubisoft. The studio confirmed the content is real and stated that it would reveal more on September 10.

Fans have started to connect the dots that this may be the date of the next Nintendo Direct. Historically, Ubisoft shows off the dancing franchise during Nintendo Directs in September, and Nintendo tends to hold these Directs around the date mentioned in Ubisoft's post.

Hello Dancers, we are sharing an important message with you today. pic.twitter.com/Z0hFuKUVIz — Just Dance (@justdancegame) August 27, 2026

Hello Dancers, we are sharing an important message with you today. pic.twitter.com/Z0hFuKUVIz

Of course, this is just speculation, but it would track based on Nintendo's history. The company is overdue for some news on The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, and Sony is also gearing up for a State of Play later this week . It's not uncommon for the two companies to have presentations back to back like this, though that is often coincidental.

Should this come to fruition, it means we will get a Nintendo Direct next Thursday, and we'll likely hear more about it early next week. It's unclear what else might show up at the Nintendo Direct, but you can likely expect a big focus on the Ocarina of Time remake , since that releases in November. We may also get a tease of what's on the horizon for 2027, but we'll just have to wait and see.

Players will be able to access the new live TV feature on their PlayStation 5 devices at an unspecified point later today. According to Sony, all you have to do is navigate to the console's Media tab, select "Live TV on PS5" while signed into a PlayStation Network account, and voila! You can see a 30-second introduction video for the surprise feature below.

Sony did a much better job of detailing the specific entertainment PS5 owners can take advantage of with a full breakdown on its site. You can see everything you need to know below.

Movies – Free movies across action, horror, sci-fi and more, with channels including MovieSphere by Lionsgate, 50 Cent Action, FilmRise Free Movies, Sony One Horror Hits and Cinevault.

"We hope you enjoy this new easy way to discover and watch free entertainment directly on PS5," Sony said.

Sony furthed detailed Live TV on PS5 in an FAQ section for the feature's new, official page . In case there was any confusion here, the company makes it clear: "Live TV on PS5 is completely free." Both live and on-demand content will be available at launch, too.

articles.title: Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet Has Finished Shooting Its Performance Capture, Confirms Naughty Dog
articles.summary: Naughty Dog's next game, Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, has wrapped shooting on the game's performance capture.
articles.body:
Naughty Dog's next game, Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet , has wrapped shooting its performance capture.

Naughty Dog confirmed in a new social media post that Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet has concluded its "cinematic shoot." This means that all of the story content has been captured by the actors and likely suggests that the game is entering its final stages. Performance capture often takes years, with actors performing the game in chunks as the team simultaneously continues to create the game.

"See you, space cowboy..." That is a wrap on the very ambitious Intergalactic cinematic shoot! This cast killed it! Cannot wait to show you their incredible work when the time is right! pic.twitter.com/WgqgcHGm8K — Naughty Dog (@Naughty_Dog) August 31, 2026

"See you, space cowboy..." That is a wrap on the very ambitious Intergalactic cinematic shoot! This cast killed it! Cannot wait to show you their incredible work when the time is right! pic.twitter.com/WgqgcHGm8K

For reference, The Last of Us Part 2 wrapped performance capture in April 2019 , roughly a year before the game's release in June 2020. However, Naughty Dog had initially planned for that game to release in February 2020 before a delay pushed it to May 2020. Once COVID happened, the game was briefly delayed once more to June 2020.

With that said, it's possible that Intergalactic is just a year away from launch. A 2027 release has been rumored and speculated for a while, but nothing has been confirmed by Naughty Dog. There is a PlayStation State of Play later this week , so it's possible that Naughty Dog will share new details on the game there. It has been nearly two years since the title was announced, and Naughty Dog hasn't said much about it since its reveal.

Fans have also been frustrated that Naughty Dog hasn't had a game since 2020, but that was never part of the plan. The studio was meant to release The Last of Us Online between The Last of Us 2 and Intergalactic , but its cancellation created a more significant gap in releases for the studio. Going forward, there likely won't be big generational gaps as Naughty Dog has multiple projects in development, which are speculated to be Uncharted 5 and The Last of Us Part 3 .

articles.title: Shailene Woodley Reflects on Cut Mary Jane Role in The Amazing Spider-Man 2
articles.summary: Actress Shailene Woodley reflects on playing Mary Jane Watson in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 before her scenes were cut from the final film.
articles.body:
You may recall that Shailene Woodley was cast as Mary Jane Watson in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 . The Divergent and Big Little Lies actor shot her scenes opposite Andrew Garfield’s wall-crawler for what she now calls her “dream” role in the Marvel-Sony sequel, only to later find out she had been cut from the movie entirely before it hit theaters in 2014.

In a recent chat with the SAG-AFTRA Foundation’s Conversations (via The Hollywood Reporter ), Woodley recalled her disappointment when she learned a year after she’d shot her scenes that she had been cut from Amazing Spider-Man 2.

“I was cast as Mary Jane for Spider-Man, which was my dream. Oh my god, Spider-Man’s my favorite superhero; Mary Jane was my favorite character growing up. So, when I got it, I was like, ‘This is so exciting!'” Woodley said.

“We filmed like three scenes together, me and Andrew Garfield. And then, like a year later, they were like, ‘So, you’re not in the movie anymore.’ And I was like, ‘What? What do you mean?’ And they’re like, ‘We’ve introduced a lot of new characters in this last one, and we’re going to wait for whatever happens between [Emma Stone’s Gwen Stacy] and Andrew [Garfield].'”

“They were like, ‘Let’s wait for her to die, and then we’ll introduce Mary Jane.’ Which made sense, but then they didn’t make that film. So, there was no reintroduction,” Woodley said. “That’s what I was told, but again, who knows what the truth is? I could have been terrible, and they were like, ‘We can’t do this.'”

The Amazing Spider-Man 2 ends with the death of Emma Stone’s Gwen Stacy, and the filmmakers said at the time that was one reason they cut Woodley’s Mary Jane from the movie.

“Shailene is a brilliant actress, and she did a great couple days of work,” director Marc Webb said. “But it was very difficult to introduce someone as a competing love interest when so much is on the table with Peter and Gwen.”

“We bit off more than we can chew,” said producer Matt Tolmach. “We had a superhero opera, and as great as Shailene is, she didn’t really co-exist with the bigger story we were telling.

"You can’t have Peter thinking about Gwen every moment, and then there’s this girl next door who’s suddenly there. We weren’t ready for it.”

Every Upcoming Spider-Man Movie Spin-Off in Development

Any chance of Woodley reprising her role as Mary Jane Watson in The Amazing Spider-Man 3 never came to pass. Sony Pictures and Marvel rebooted the franchise instead with Tom Holland as the new Spidey and Zendaya as the MCU’s version of MJ. Sony then produced a series of increasingly unsuccessful Spidey villain spin-offs, but the studio recently shelved plans for any more of those.

articles.title: Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons Gameplay Reveal Gives Extended Look at Combat, Exploration, and Traversal
articles.body:
Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons recently released its long-awaited gameplay reveal at gamescom, and it gave us an extended look at main character Kaatri and the powers she has at her disposal.

If you weren’t already aware, Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons is a single-player, third-person, open-world action-adventure game from developer Invoke Studios where you wield forbidden magic to bend the rules, outwit obstacles, and overcome challenges through creativity. Kaatri is the warlock, and the gameplay reveal begins with her and Tasha, her witch queen patron. We see Tasha upgrade Kaatri’s Warlock’s Eye, which allows her to see Raw Magic and is the key to finding new spells and improving the ones she has.

From there, Kaatri moves to Darkon, a Domain of Dread pulled directly from D&D. It’s unstable and on the verge of being ripped apart by Mists. There is time to explore Darkon, but it’s filled with danger and opportunity around every corner.

Exploration is clearly a big focus of Warlock. As you travel through Darkon, you’ll need to stay alert and use magic to help you make your way. Your Warlock’s Eye will point you toward Raw Magic, but it’ll be up to you to figure out what to do with it. You need to pay attention to the sights and sounds around you and decide what deserves your attention.

Kaatri heads into Crickshank, a settlement in Darkon that harbors a dark secret that players can uncover. Skev, her imp companion, flies alongside as Crickshank's biggest mystery pulls them underground, beneath its shops. Kaatri enters the ossuary catacombs, and we see her utilize both her dexterity and magic for rapid traversal.

She emerges into a large chamber full of monsters, including the eyeball-like aberration Death Kiss. Kaatri rushes into combat and uses a spell to latch onto a column and pull it down onto a monster. The developers have revealed that this spell is called Tasha’s Leash and is a brand-new cantrip that can be used to pull or throw objects whenever you want, showing that use of the environment will be a major part of combat.

With the Death Kiss closing in on her, Kaatri then uses another spell to swap positions with a different monster, allowing her to escape to high ground while the Death Kiss destroys the monster she swapped with. The developers shared that this is called Fey Switch, a new Warlock advanced spell.

These new spells are all well and good, but if you’ve played D&D before, you know there’s one tried and true spell that’s a mainstay for all Warlocks: Eldritch Blast. So of course, we get a look at that too. As with its D&D counterpart, Eldritch Blast’s value in Warlock is its versatility. It’s a cantrip, so it’s consistently available. And it’s helpful in just about any situation, whether you need a ranged attack to apply pressure to an enemy, want to cleanly finish one off, or want to keep your offensive momentum going in between melee strikes and bigger spells. It’s a key part of your kit, just as it should be.

The gameplay reveal then shows another way you can use the environment: weather. Kaatri makes her way into a misty field and invokes the Downpour Ritual, calling forth rain and forming puddles across a field where vampires are fighting a horde of zombies. Kaatri casts Witch Bolt, shooting out electricity that spreads across the wet surfaces and forks through enemies.

Since she’s a Pact of the Blade Warlock, Kaatri is then able to conjure a sword and other pact weapons to switch into melee combat. And that’s where it all comes together, as Kaatri weaves together magical and melee combat and showcases the core of Warlock’s combat system. The effects of one spell can feed into the next, as you chain together different abilities depending on the enemies you’re facing and the space you’re in.

The video ends with Kaatri finding a Strand of Magic, giving us a glimpse at the Raw Magic that’s hidden across Darkon that will fuel Kaatri’s progression throughout the game. It’s clear that Warlock draws on familiar spells, locations, and lore that D&D fans will immediately recognize, but tells a new and original story that newcomers can dive into and learn everything they need to know.

Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons is slated to release on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S in 2027. To get the latest news and updates, you can check out the game’s official website or follow it on Instagram , Twitter , TikTok , Facebook , or YouTube . And for more coverage of the game as we get more info, stay tuned to IGN.

articles.title: PlayStation Claims Digital Games Are Not Really Owned by Players in Response to Class-Action Lawsuit
articles.summary: Sony has given a divisive response to a class-action lawsuit that argues the PlayStation online store doesn’t make it obvious enough that players are merely purchasing a revocable license to play a game, and not the game itself.
articles.body:
Sony has given a divisive response to a class-action lawsuit that argues the PlayStation online store doesn’t make it obvious enough that players are merely purchasing a revocable license to play a game, rather than owning the entire game itself.

The lawsuit, filed on June 18, 2026, says PlayStation “fails to clearly and conspicuously disclose to consumers at the point of sale that these transactions do not convey ownership of the digital games.” It argues that the company “relegates this information to inconspicuous text or separate agreements that consumers are not required to affirmatively acknowledge.”

This, at least, is true; before checking out on PlayStation’s digital storefront, a message is displayed in small text that reads: "By selecting [Confirm Purchase], you agree to complete the purchase in accordance with the PlayStation Terms of Service before using this content. You further acknowledge that your purchase of this digital product amounts to a license subject to the Software Product License Agreement.”

PlayStation has now provided its retort to this lawsuit. In an August 21 filing in California’s Northern District Court, it argues that it has done enough to make it obvious that customers are simply buying a license, rather than the full game for their permanent ownership.

“As Plaintiffs admit, Section 1 of the SPLA likewise explains that ‘The Software is licensed to you, not sold.’ This makes sense. In the digital age, it is not plausible to allege that reasonable consumers believed they were obtaining ‘ownership’ of a digital game. Were that the case, then Plaintiff Edward Heycock would not have been able to obtain the game Resident Evil Requiem on February 25, 2026 for $69.99 from the PlayStation Store after Plaintiff Jason Mendoza had obtained Resident Evil Requiem on February 14, 2026, because Mr. Mendoza, not Sony, would have owned it then," the company's response reads.

Needless to say, this reply has sparked a fierce wave of backlash from players on social media, who are already riled up over Sony’s decision to end the production of physical game discs starting January 2028. With this context in mind, many feel Sony’s counterargument is downright malicious: If the company continues to pursue an all-digital future, then players will truly own nothing outright, as the game licenses on Sony’s digital storefront can simply be yanked away at any time.

“‘The Software is licensed to you, not sold.’ Then why does the page say I'm ‘Buying’ it? Sounds like false advertisement to me,” one wrote on X.

“They can't simply take away your full game if you have the full file installed and it’s working and complete without the need of servers, and also can't make unaccessible or unplayable for no reason,” another argued.

“The United States needs to pass a law to catch up with the era of digital media. I should be able to own what is sold to me, and I should be able to do whatever I want to do with what I own,” another urged .

If “license” is being used as the legal mechanism that transforms an ordinary purchase into a restricted permission, shouldn't the law define what a consumer license actually is, rather than allowing every publisher to construct its own version and then rely on the same word to… — aCat (@Alex1Ne0) August 29, 2026

If “license” is being used as the legal mechanism that transforms an ordinary purchase into a restricted permission, shouldn't the law define what a consumer license actually is, rather than allowing every publisher to construct its own version and then rely on the same word to…

“The Software is licensed to you, not sold.” Then why does the page says I'm "Buying" it? sounds like false advertisement to me. pic.twitter.com/bvIz5J4iy9 — Backlog Dragon - Gaming VTuber (@BacklogDragon) August 29, 2026

“The Software is licensed to you, not sold.” Then why does the page says I'm "Buying" it? sounds like false advertisement to me. pic.twitter.com/bvIz5J4iy9

If a company sells you a digital license, it must guarantee permanent access to a downloadable copy of the licensed product If the company shuts down, abandons the product, or goes bankrupt, the game must automatically be transferred to an independent digital archive, together… — Rage Crusader (@RageCrusader) August 29, 2026

If a company sells you a digital license, it must guarantee permanent access to a downloadable copy of the licensed product If the company shuts down, abandons the product, or goes bankrupt, the game must automatically be transferred to an independent digital archive, together…

This argument is at the heart of another lawsuit the company is facing in Mexico. Brought forward in July, Mexican lawmakers allege that PlayStation is engaging in “anti-competitive practices” by choosing to end physical disc production, as it would severely limit competition from independent games retailers by forcing players to go through its digital storefront if they want to play PlayStation games.

PlayStation's online store is central to another lawsuit in the Netherlands, where Dutch Consumer Group Stichting Massaschade & Consument argues that its customers are getting charged more for digital games in comparison to customers in different countries.

Sony, for its part, has made no move to renege on its choice to kill physical games. In July, the company's chief financial officer, Lin Tao, said it will "cautiously move this forward" with this plan, claiming that it is keeping players' high emotions around the topic in "consideration."

"In the future digital ecosystem, how do we engage the gamers is something that we would like to continue to explore," she said.

You can play locally in split-screen, or online using either GameShare or the Orbitals Global Friend’s Pass . Either way, you only need one copy of the game to play with a friend, which is pretty neat.

Starting earlier this year, Nintendo began charging different prices for digital and physical Switch 2 games. Now, physical games cost $10 more than digital games on the eShop. However, both Walmart and Amazon have been offering physical versions of most of those games for $10 less than elsewhere, eliminating the difference. In the case of Orbitals, Amazon has sold out of preorders.

September is packed with major releases. In addition to Orbitals launching on September 3, The Blood of Dawnwalker is also out that day (we gave it a 9/10 in our review ). Then, on Friday, September 4, Onimusha: Way of the Sword comes out (we gave it a 10/10 in our review ). And that's just this week. Later in September, we'll see the release of Marvel's Wolverine, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, Control Resonant, Silent Hill Townfall, Minecraft Dungeons 2, and The Witcher 3 Remastered.

It’s a crowded month because nearly all publishers with fall games have shifted their release dates into September or October in order to get out of the way of Grand Theft Auto VI. GTA 6 launches November 19, with preloads starting a week earlier. That game certainly looks great, but it seems like some other games could come out in November if they were brave enough. Alas, it’s mostly Godzilla and Barbie.
